pois.name: Green-Wood Cemetery
pois.short_description: 478-acre Gothic-Revival garden cemetery in Brooklyn (chartered 1838); a Victorian rural cemetery and one of America's first urban parks, holding ~600,000 interments including Currier, Tiffany, Howe, Bernstein, and DeWitt Clinton.

beats.script_body: When Green-Wood was chartered on April 18, 1838, Manhattan's churchyard cemeteries were filling fast and the island was running out of room, while newly incorporated Brooklyn had fewer than sixteen thousand residents and an abundance of unused land. The story begins with Henry Evelyn Pierrepont, scion of one of Brooklyn's most prominent families, who visited Cambridge, Massachusetts, to study the newly opened Mount Auburn Cemetery — the first planned, nondenominational, rural cemetery in America. He toured Europe looking for a model, and returned with an image of a sprawling garden cemetery for Manhattan. His idea was dismissed as a waste of valuable real estate. So he turned to Brooklyn, where he saw the chance to build a city like the great cities of Europe, with wide promenades, public squares, and a grand cemetery. When the City of Brooklyn began laying out its streets in 1835, it made no provision for a cemetery at all. Pierrepont gathered citizens who petitioned the state legislature for a charter, and the Hills of Gowanus, where you now stand, were selected as the site. Within a year the Green-Wood Corporation purchased nearly two hundred acres of grazing land at $750 per acre — a total of $134,650 — from the Wyckoff, Ibbotson, Dean, Sackett, Schermerhorn, Bennett, and Bergen families.

beats.source_passage: When Green-Wood Cemetery was chartered on April 18, 1838, New York City was already the commercial and financial center of America and, with a population of more than three hundred thousand, its largest city. Manhattan churchyard cemeteries were rapidly filling and the island was quickly running out of available space. But newly incorporated Brooklyn had fewer than sixteen thousand residents and an abundance of unused land. Our story begins when Henry Evelyn Pierrepont (1808–1888), scion of one of Brooklyn's most prominent families, visited Cambridge, Massachusetts, to study the newly opened Mount Auburn Cemetery, the first planned, nondenominational, rural cemetery in America. He then toured Europe, looking for a cemetery model to bring to Manhattan. Pierrepont returned from Europe with an image of a sprawling garden cemetery for Manhattan. His idea was dismissed as a waste of valuable real estate. He turned to Brooklyn and saw the opportunity to create a city like the great cities of Europe—with wide promenades, public squares, and a grand cemetery. The Hills of Gowanus, where you now stand, were selected as the site. Within a year, the Green-Wood Corporation, organized by Pierrepont plus other prominent Brooklynites, purchased nearly two hundred acres of grazing land at $750per acre, for a total of $134,650, from the Wyckoff, Ibbotson, Dean, Sackett, Schermerhorn, Bennett, and Bergen families.

beats.script_body: To turn this grazing pasture into a cemetery, the corporation hired David Bates Douglass, who had served in the War of 1812 and taught mathematics and engineering at West Point, and had been chief engineer for the Croton Aqueduct System — he designed the High Bridge that still carries Croton's water across the Harlem River. One of his first tasks was to lay out 4.5 miles of road following the contours of the terrain. This route became known as "the Tour," designed to display Green-Wood's charms and to tempt potential lot buyers. The unexpected side effect: Green-Wood quickly became a major recreational and tourist destination for New Yorkers, who had almost no public parkland at all. Douglass even had songbirds imported from Europe to help set the ambiance.

beats.source_passage: David Bates Douglass (1790–1849) was hired the next month to transform this grazing pasture into a cemetery. Douglass had served in the War of 1812and had been a professor of mathematics and engineering at the United States Military Academy. Before working on Green-Wood, he had also been the chief engineer for the Croton Aqueduct System. Among other things he designed the High Bridge, which remains the oldest bridge still standing in the city, to transport Croton's water across the Harlem River to Manhattan. One of Douglass's first tasks was to lay out 4.5miles of road that followed the contours of the terrain and demonstrated the beauty of the site. This route became known as "the Tour" and was designed and used not only to display Green-Wood's charms but also to serve as an incentive for potential lot buyers. One unexpected side effect of the Tour was that Green-Wood quickly became a major recreational and tourist destination for New Yorkers, who had access to almost no public parkland at all. Douglass even had songbirds imported from Europe to assist with the ambiance.

beats.script_body: The early years were lean: from the first interment on September 5, 1840, to the end of 1842, only 162 burials took place; by 1843 the total had crept to 352. Then 1844 brought a dramatic change — 354 people were buried in that single year and lot sales hit $20,000. Three things drove the boom: growing acceptance of nondenominational burial, an easing of the 1837 depression that left people more disposable income, and the relocation of former senator, governor, and mayor DeWitt Clinton's casket from Albany to Green-Wood, which signaled that the wealthy classes had embraced the place. By 1855, just fifteen years after the first burial, 45,576 people had been interred and over a hundred thousand visitors were coming annually.

beats.script_body: Wary New Yorkers thought a distant cemetery seemed insecure, so Green-Wood enclosed itself with a two-mile fence. The current fence, some 21,120 feet long, went up beginning in 1860 at a cost of $40,000. Note its decorative cast-iron finials capping each post. In 2000 the cemetery launched a campaign to restore 280 missing finials — at a price near $50,000, more than the entire original fence cost.

beats.script_body: The tour begins at the dramatic Gothic Revival gates designed by architect Richard Upjohn, built between 1861 and 1863, once Green-Wood was an established success and its trustees wanted an imposing entrance. Upjohn was one of America's most renowned nineteenth-century architects, working mainly in Greek and Gothic Revival and specializing in churches — his greatest surviving New York work is Trinity Church at Broadway and Wall Street. He later helped found the American Institute of Architects with Richard Morris Hunt. Gothic Revival was a perfect match for Green-Wood: it celebrated mystery, illusion, and the inherent irregularity of nature itself. The gates are a splendid example. The center tower stands 106 feet tall, flanked by two 90-foot peaks, the symmetry counterbalanced by office wings of differing shapes and sizes. They are built of red sandstone from Belleville, New Jersey — the same material Upjohn used for Trinity Church — and crowded with steep slate roofs, stone trefoils and quatrefoils, cast-iron bannerettes, open gables, and detailed finials. Embedded above the entranceways are four reliefs carved by John M. Moffitt in Nova Scotia yellow sandstone, symbolizing rebirth and resurrection: "Come Forth," "The Dead Shall Be Raised," "I Am the Resurrection and the Life," and "Weep Not." Higher up are smaller reliefs of Faith, Hope, Memory, and Love. In 1966 the main gates were designated a New York City landmark.

beats.script_body: This tomb brings together two of the greatest artists of the late nineteenth century: it was designed by architect Stanford White, and the bronzes were created in 1883 by Augustus Saint-Gaudens. It holds Pennsylvania coal and steel magnate David Stewart, the father of Isabella Stewart Gardner, doyenne of Boston's art scene. The reliefs depict two robed angels — highly controversial at the time, because most depictions of death were gloomy and despairing, while White showed his angels as musicians, perhaps heralding the ascension to heaven. With little patience for the criticism, White wrote to Saint-Gaudens that "some people are such God damned asses they always think of death as a gloomy performance instead of a resurrection."

beats.script_body: A few feet farther along Battle Avenue, on the other side of the road, a marble marker with a large cross carries the bronze emblem of the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. This is the grave of Louis Bonnard, a French émigré who developed and patented profitable inventions — a mechanical brick maker, a machine for molding cast iron — in the cellar workshop of his Mulberry Street tenement. As he lay near death, Bonnard became convinced he would be resurrected as an animal and could be abused. He sent for Henry Bergh, founder of the ASPCA, and promised his fortune to the newly established organization. Bergh arrived to find his benefactor living in abject poverty. Bonnard told him he was leaving everything to the ASPCA, then asked the skeptical Bergh to open a trunk in the room — and Bergh found it filled with money and jewels. Bonnard's family disputed the bequest, claiming the inventor was insane, but the courts upheld the donation, and the ASPCA became one of the best-endowed charities in New York.

beats.script_body: This tall obelisk was erected by the City of Brooklyn to memorialize the 278 people who died in the Brooklyn Theater Fire on December 5, 1876; 103 of the victims are buried here. Theater was a main source of entertainment in nineteenth-century America, and that Tuesday evening more than a thousand patrons had gathered at the Brooklyn Theater downtown to watch star Kate Claxton in the popular Two Orphans. As the play was ending, around 11 p.m., someone told Claxton that a kerosene lamp had ignited a small fire in the scenery backstage. With the actors unsure what to do, Claxton supposedly whispered, "Go on, they will put it out, if we say anything there will be panic, go on." The fire couldn't be contained. As the audience realized, Claxton tried to reassure them — "We are between you and the flames" — but patrons fled in panic, clogging the few narrow exits. Within half an hour the roof collapsed and 278 lives were lost. The City of Brooklyn dug a seven-foot-deep, crescent-shaped common grave for the unidentified and the families who could not afford burial; 103 donated coffins were arranged with heads facing the center, and two thousand mourners attended with song, speeches, and flowers.

beats.script_body: Across Battle Avenue from the theater-fire monument stand the graves of Henry Aaron Burr and his family. Henry Aaron Burr was the great-nephew of the infamous vice president Aaron Burr and a nephew of minister Jonathan Edwards — but he was famous in his own right as an innovator in the hat industry. After working as a bookkeeper for milliner Elisha Bloomer, Burr opened his own store across the street in 1835 and set out to perfect a machine for forming hats. After many failures he succeeded, patented it, and dramatically cut the cost of hat making; by 1856 millions of his machines were in use worldwide. The invention was so successful he was forced to sue for patent infringement fifty-six times, winning all but three. Burr was also a charter member of the Union Club and a director of the Mechanics' National Bank.

beats.script_body: Along Syringa Path, to your left, lies the Uhl-Ottendorfer family plot. Anna and Jacob Uhl started the Staats-Zeitung — the City Paper — as a German weekly in New York in December 1834. When Jacob died in 1851, his widow Anna took over the paper, and in 1859 she married Oswald Ottendorfer, a German immigrant who had worked there over a decade. Under them the Staats-Zeitung became the preeminent German-language paper in New York, reaching a circulation of sixty-five thousand by 1880, and it ran as a daily until 1975. The Ottendorfers gave away much of their fortune to German American causes, including a free library whose building still stands on Second Avenue near Tenth Street in Manhattan. They are one of many newspaper families buried here — Henry Raymond of the Times, Horace Greeley of the Tribune, and J. Gordon Bennett of the Herald also rest in Green-Wood.

beats.script_body: On a small grass island stands the imposing statue of DeWitt Clinton, his back to you as you approach. Clinton was a remarkable man — son of Revolutionary War general James Clinton, he chose government over the military, became personal secretary to his uncle Governor George Clinton around 1790, and within a decade was one of New York State's most powerful politicians. Appointed to the U.S. Senate in 1802, he returned the next year to serve as mayor of New York, holding that office, with two brief breaks, until 1815. As mayor he oversaw the creation of the New-York Historical Society and the Orphan Asylum, sanitation improvements, the 1811 street-grid system, and the fortification of the harbor before the War of 1812. He ran for president in 1812, losing to James Madison by a slim margin, and served three terms as governor. But he is best remembered as the "Father of the Erie Canal" for his tireless support of the project that assured New York's commercial dominance; he presided over its 1825 opening. His statue was cast by Henry Kirke Brown between 1850 and 1853, the base designed by Richard Upjohn, and was displayed in Manhattan's City Hall Park before being placed here. Two bronze reliefs on the base depict the building of the canal.

beats.script_body: Sharing Clinton's small island of grass, a few feet to the south among the trees, is Nathaniel Currier — senior partner of the lithography firm Currier and Ives. In the second half of the nineteenth century the firm produced thousands of images for mass consumption; their work was excellent, but it was their unparalleled marketing that made them the nation's most successful lithographers. His partner, James Merritt Ives, is buried elsewhere in Green-Wood.

beats.script_body: Opposite Clinton's tomb, a small white marble statue of a young man marks the grave of three-year-old Irwin Franklin, "Little Frankie." It was carved by the great American sculptor Daniel Chester French, best known for the seated Lincoln at the Lincoln Memorial. Frankie, who died in 1880, was the son of Rear Admiral Aaron Ward; father and son lie buried adjacent to each other. Such carving was often the "bread and butter" of master sculptors between large commissions.

beats.script_body: Downhill off Fern Avenue stands the Greek Revival tomb of John Anderson, four columns in a style popular in antebellum America, built by Anderson himself in the early 1860s, twenty years before his death. Anderson owned a tobacco shop on Broadway across from City Hall Park, selling his "fine cut" Anderson's Solace Tobacco. In 1838 he hired an attractive young woman, Mary Cecilia Rogers, to draw young men to the shop, and she soon picked up the nickname "the Beautiful Seegar Girl." In July 1842, Mary disappeared; three days later she turned up floating in the Hudson River, and Anderson became the prime suspect. He was arrested, questioned, and immediately released, the details hushed up by influential friends in the Democratic Party — and his was the only statement among the questioned men not released to the press. The murder of Mary Rogers was one of the first crimes sensationalized by the New York papers, the Herald, Sun, and Tribune competing to spin a "real-life mystery." Rumors that she died from a botched abortion led the state senate to criminalize the practice, and the failure to solve the crime led to the Police Reform Act of 1845. Her story also became the basis for Edgar Allan Poe's The Mystery of Marie Roget. After her death Anderson gave away much of his fortune. The story outlived him: his daughter contested his will, claiming he was insane and believed Mary Rogers's ghost visited him regularly and that Garibaldi's ghost inhabited his house. A witness testified Anderson had said his house was haunted — "by people who want money." His daughter lost.

beats.script_body: About ten feet behind the Mulberry Avenue street sign stands the grave of Colonel Abraham Vosburgh, its column carved with an eagle holding a sword — a reference to his military service — and broken, marking a life cut short. On April 22, 1861, Vosburgh marched at the head of the Seventy-first New York State National Guard toward Washington, answering Lincoln's plea to defend the capital. Without seeing any action, he died of consumption in Washington. After President Lincoln laid a wreath on his body, the colonel was returned to Brooklyn for burial. His regiment erected this monument, inscribed "Pro Patria" — For Country — originally ringed by a cast-iron fence with posts shaped like bayoneted rifles and a gate topped with a Union cap, belt, and sword. That fence has since disappeared. Vosburgh is far from the only officer here: from the Civil War alone Green-Wood holds nearly twenty generals from both sides and thirteen Medal of Honor recipients.

beats.script_body: The Burnham burial site is a classic late nineteenth-century family plot, with a central monument crowned by an imposing statue, sculpted by John Moffitt, of a woman in classical dress holding a Bible, the whole ringed by a stone wall that replaced a decayed iron fence. Gordon W. Burnham earned his millions as president of the Waterbury Clock, Waterbury Watch, and American Pin companies. He is buried here with his first two wives. He died shortly before a third marriage: he caught a chill waiting in his unheated carriage for his fiancée Kate Sanborn's ferry, which ran an hour late; the chill became pneumonia, and he died three days before the wedding. A staunch Democrat, Burnham had delayed that wedding until after the March 4 inauguration of Grover Cleveland — so as not to be married under a Republican administration.

beats.script_body: A short detour off Battle Avenue leads to the free-standing mausoleum of Marcus "Copper King" Daly — be sure to note the magnificent stained-glass windows at the rear. Born in Ireland, Daly came to America at fifteen with virtually no money. In 1880, after years of struggling, he scraped together enough to buy a small mine near Butte, Montana. Nominally a silver mine, in places its veins ran 55 percent copper — and Daly had hit the mother lode just as Thomas Edison was using copper to wire his new electric lights. His Anaconda Mining Company was soon joined by California financiers, and together they bought up neighboring claims until Daly's mines controlled nearly a quarter of the world's mined copper. About twenty-five miles from Butte he built the company town of Anaconda, diversified into coal and lumber, and became a millionaire several times over. Daly was deeply active in Montana Democratic politics and at constant war with his mining rival Andrew Clark; the two fought with money and the press for control of the state. Clark's ambition was to become a U.S. senator; Daly's was simply to stop Clark. Clark spent $450,000 to keep the capital out of Daly's Anaconda — and he won that fight, and ultimately the Senate seat, but not until 1901, after Daly's death.

beats.script_body: Up the steps marked "Battle Path" stands Green-Wood's Soldiers' Monument, erected in 1869 to honor the 148,000 New York men who fought "in aid of the war for the preservation of the Union and the Constitution." Built just four years after the war's end, it is far more realistic in its vision of battle than the nostalgic memorials of the 1880s and 1890s, when the blood and guts had faded from memory. Its four life-size soldiers — supposedly cast from the bronze of captured Confederate cannons — represent the Union Army. They originally held an ax, rifle, rammer, and sword, now all missing. In 1991 the four relief battle scenes on the central monument, which had been stolen, were refabricated and replaced.

beats.script_body: Near granite marker 18495 lies a low white gravestone whose only inscription is "Grandmother." This is the grave of Elizabeth Tilton. She had been married to Theodore Tilton and was a schoolteacher for the Reverend Henry Ward Beecher of Plymouth Church in Brooklyn Heights. She and Beecher had an affair, exposed by Victoria Woodhull; Theodore sued Beecher for "alienation of affection," and the story became national news. Beecher claimed victory with a hung jury, but the family was torn apart by the "trial of the century." Theodore left the United States in 1883 and spent his life in Paris; Elizabeth was ostracized by everyone but her daughter and a few religious friends, and died alone and blind in 1897. Her marker reads simply "Grandmother" in an attempt to keep tourists from invading her final resting place. Beecher stayed with his wife and lies in a prominent tomb elsewhere in Green-Wood.

beats.script_body: Minerva and the Altar to Liberty, sculpted by F. Wellington Ruxell, was unveiled on August 27, 1920 — the 144th anniversary of the Battle of Long Island, fought on this very spot in late August 1776. In Greek mythology Minerva, also known as Pallas Athena, whose temple is the Parthenon, sprang fully formed and armored from Zeus's head; she was the goddess of battle and protector of civilized life. The battle she marks was the first for the Continental army after the Declaration of Independence some seven weeks earlier. Two thousand American troops under Brigadier General William Alexander — called Lord Stirling by his men — fought Major General James Grant's British force three times larger. Much of the fighting swept across the ridge where you now stand, which is why it is called Battle Hill; it is said that atop this hill a group of American riflemen were surrounded, shot, and buried where they fell. The Greek Revival tomb directly behind Minerva is that of Charles M. Higgins, a Park Slope businessman and inventor of India ink, whose ambition was to build a memorial to the first battle for American freedom and who led the movement to erect the statue. This is the highest natural point in Brooklyn, 216 feet above sea level — and if you stand directly in front of Minerva, you'll see her left hand raised in salute to the Statue of Liberty, standing due west in New York harbor.

beats.script_body: Along Liberty Path, among two evergreen shrubs to your right, are the unassuming graves of Leonard Bernstein, his wife, and his sister. Born in Lawrence, Massachusetts, Bernstein conducted the New York City Symphony Orchestra from 1945 to 1948 and was with the New York Philharmonic from 1957 until being named conductor laureate in 1969. He was the first conductor to use television successfully as a tool for music education, and a prolific composer — his best-known piece is the 1957 musical West Side Story. His grave is usually piled with small stones: it is a Jewish tradition to leave a stone when visiting, to honor the person buried, both to pay homage and to record your presence. Stones, related to the ground, last far longer than flowers.

beats.script_body: Behind Higgins, hidden in a grove of trees, is the Edwin C. Litchfield plot. Litchfield was a prominent Brooklyn lawyer and businessman who, with his brother Electus, developed Brooklyn's street railways and the Gowanus Canal and acquired a large tract from the Cortelyou estate that they turned into Park Slope. He also played a prominent role in creating Prospect Park. In 1892, after his death, his family estate — Grace Hill — was converted into the Parks Department building inside the park and renamed Litchfield Villa in his honor. The rumor is that his grave is turned away from Park Slope, to protest the taking of his family home by the Parks Department.

beats.script_body: At the intersection of Battle and Hemlock Avenues stands the imposing Howe family grave site, overseen by a bust of the patriarch, Elias Howe Jr. Born to a large, impoverished Massachusetts family, Howe went to work at six and never had a formal education. In 1846 he patented the first sewing machine. It was grossly inefficient, but it sewed 250 stitches a minute — five times faster than a skilled hand. Sewers and tailors fearing for their jobs met it with resistance, and manufacturers were reluctant to spend on machinery when cheap human labor was abundant. Realizing America wasn't ready, Howe went to England to market it, and returned two years later penniless — only to discover his invention had been stolen. After five years of litigation he won his patent suit, securing protection for the lockstitch formed by his eye-pointed needle and mechanical shuttle, and thereafter collected a royalty on every sewing machine made in America: his income rose from $300 a year to $200,000 — over $5 million today. Directly behind Howe is buried the family dog, Fannie, who died in 1881, her marble marker carved with a poem that begins, "Only a dog you say sir critic."

beats.script_body: On the near right corner of the small Lake Path is the tombstone of William Kingsley, a Brooklyn contractor and one of the earliest proponents of building a bridge between Brooklyn and Manhattan. In 1865, at age thirty-two, he hired engineer Colonel Julius Walker Adams to draw up a design and cost estimates; Adams figured the bridge could be built for about $5 million. The Kingsley bridge was never built — in the end the Roebling bridge cost $15 million. Kingsley was a leader of Brooklyn's Democratic machine, and the Brooklyn Bridge project made him nearly a million dollars alone, perhaps thanks to his association with Manhattan "Boss" William M. Tweed. When the Tweed ring was broken in 1873, it emerged that Kingsley, a major stockholder and general superintendent of the project, was being paid 15 percent of total construction expenses — over $170,000 a year — a payment made, per the Bridge Company's records, at Tweed's suggestion. After Tweed's fall his salary was renegotiated to a flat $10,000; without that change he would have garnered roughly $1.75 million by the bridge's 1883 completion. Fittingly, his grave marker was cut from a granite stone taken from the Brooklyn Bridge itself, placed here by the bridge trustees to commemorate his role in making the Great Bridge a reality.

The shattered trunk symbolizes a young life abruptly ended; the books and globe, his life as a student; the Union uniform and rifle, perhaps a soldier's ambitions never realized.

beats.script_body: Green-Wood's grave markers are a catalog of Victorian funerary art, illustrating Christian ideas of ascension, resurrection, and salvation. A few to look for: an intertwined alpha and omega — the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, from Revelation, "the beginning and the end." The phrase Fugit Hora — "the hours are fleeting," or "time flies." Animals recur: an eagle is a heavenly messenger or a sign of military service; a butterfly is Christian metamorphosis and resurrection; a lamb — purity and innocence — is the most common nineteenth-century symbol on children's graves. Among objects, the anchor is an early Christian symbol of salvation and hope, and also of death at sea; a broken column or tree trunk marks a young life shortened; an orb means resurrection; drapery over an urn signifies mourning.

beats.script_body: On the near right corner where Green-Bough meets Fern stands the lavish white tomb of Charlotte Canda. She was the only daughter of Charles Canda, an officer in Napoleon's army who emigrated to America and ran a girls' finishing school in Manhattan. On a stormy night, February 3, 1845, a party celebrated Charlotte's seventeenth birthday. As it ended, she and her father escorted a friend home; not wanting the lady to walk alone, Charles saw her to the door, and when he returned the carriage was gone. The horse had bolted, crossed Broadway, and thrown Charlotte, who struck her head — she died just as her father reached her. The Candas were Catholic, and she was first interred in the old St. Patrick's Cathedral cemetery on Mott Street. This monument was essentially designed by Charlotte herself: she had been drawing a memorial for a recently deceased aunt, and her father found the sketch and embellished it with roses, flowers, birds, and wreaths, many repeated in the number seventeen — her age. The monument stands seventeen feet high and seventeen feet deep, incorporating her favorite things: books, musical instruments, drawing implements, and her parrot. Charlotte appears in the gown she wore the night she died, a star above her symbolizing immortal life, and a butterfly with wings extended for her liberated spirit. In the 1850s hers was the most popular grave in the cemetery, drawing thousands yearly. Just outside the consecrated ground to her right stands a monument with the coat of arms of Charles Albert Jarret de la Marie — her French fiancé, who committed suicide in the Canda residence a year after her death and could not be buried on consecrated ground, but lies as close as the church would allow.

beats.script_body: Soon after Green-Wood opened, a local paper reported visitors "began to be attracted from the city in considerable numbers daily," predicting it would become "a popular and elegant place of resort." At first they came by carriage; by the 1860s, public horsecars from downtown Brooklyn or the Fulton ferries brought them, and the cemetery began selling picture postcards and stereo cards as souvenirs. These rural cemeteries became America's first urban parks. But after public parks spread the pastoral landscape without graves, the recreational popularity of the "rural" cemetery began to wane in the last quarter of the century. Frederick Law Olmsted, who criticized the idea of cemeteries becoming "the constant resort of mere pleasure seekers," at first refused to design one — though he recanted later and designed Mountain View Cemetery in California. The Civil War's immense casualties also drained the era's sentimentalism, and the rise of art museums made cemetery-visiting less desirable.

beats.script_body: Up the hill above three small children's graves rises the mausoleum of Henry Evelyn Pierrepont, the man primarily responsible for Green-Wood. A city planner and businessman, the second son of Hezekiah B. Pierrepont, he is regarded as one of the first city planners in the United States and was active in planning Brooklyn's expansion after its 1834 incorporation; the next year he was appointed chair of a commission to lay out the new city's streets. He donated the cemetery's original fence and, in 1842, bought eight plots for himself and family. His monument, designed by Richard Upjohn, stands atop one of Green-Wood's few manmade hills. When he died, Pierrepont was the last survivor of the original trustees who created the cemetery.

beats.script_body: Off Central Avenue, a smallish marble monument with a Masonic symbol and a carved steamship honors the engineers of the monitor Weehawken. The Weehawken followed the famous armored Monitor that fought the Merrimack to a draw in 1862. Beginning in January 1863 it helped blockade the Confederate port of Charleston as part of a flotilla led by the New Ironsides. When the ironclads attacked the harbor defenses in April, at least two thousand Confederate shots rained down; the Keokuk sank, and the New Ironsides sat for an hour directly atop a torpedo holding a ton of powder that the Confederates couldn't detonate because of a broken wire. In October 1863 the Weehawken ran aground attacking Fort Sumter, and the New Ironsides put itself between her and the batteries to draw fire while Union tugs pulled her out. She was rescued — but sank two months later. Her gravestone reads: "Sacred to the memory of the officers of the United States Navy who lost their lives by being drowned on the US Monitor Weehawken... when she foundered off Charleston, SC, December 6, 1863. The remains were exhumed from the engine room of the wrecked Monitor where they nobly fell at their post of duty."

beats.script_body: Up a steep hill where Vale Path meets Central Avenue, a cluster of very simple black marble monuments marks the Tiffany family. The large central stone is patriarch Charles Lewis Tiffany, surrounded by family including his most famous son, Louis Comfort Tiffany. The internationally renowned company was founded by Charles Tiffany and partner John B. Young in 1837, selling stationery and fancy goods from a shop at 237 Broadway; after Charles bought out his partners he renamed it Tiffany and Company. His son Louis was meant to take over the business, but his talents pulled him toward the decorative arts. He studied painting in New York and Paris and traveled the world, and his great gift emerged in glass: in the 1870s he and his rival John LaFarge — also buried here — revolutionized stained glass. In 1879 Louis opened his own firm and was soon granted a patent for Favrile glass, decorating the interiors of wealthy Manhattan mansions and clubs; in 1893 he built a factory in Corona, Queens, where his Tiffany Studios produced thousands of windows, lamps, and ceramics now in museums worldwide. He even designed stained-glass windows for vaults here in Green-Wood. More interested in art than status, his grave gives only his name and dates — though note his two wives, each calling herself "Wife of Louis Comfort Tiffany, N.A.," a nod to his membership in the National Academy of Design.

beats.script_body: Along Valley Avenue, note the detailed blue-gray August Jacklitsch monument — one of the few "white bronze" memorials in Green-Wood. Only one firm, the Monumental Bronze Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, made them, casting pure zinc from the mid-1870s to roughly World War I and selling through a catalog or a sales agent with an office near the cemetery. White bronze mimicked carved marble or granite but allowed far greater detail — families could even recreate the fashionable century plant, something impossible to carve in stone. There was one problem: the monuments were mass-produced, with only the nameplates individualized and then bolted on. That made them easy for vandals to dismantle — and a handy hiding place for bootleggers to stash liquor during Prohibition.

beats.script_body: At Hillside Path stands the large monument to John "Soda Fountain King" Matthews — one of the guide's favorites. Crafted by Karl Muller in marble and terra-cotta in 1868, it was celebrated as the "Mortuary Monument of the Year." Matthews lies atop his tomb, gazing up at scenes from his life: a mix of animals, plants, the Four Evangelists, and carvings of his own children. Four corner gargoyles double as gutters, drawing rainwater off the roof. A life-size seated statue above him symbolizes grief and mourning; the center tower atop the roofline has been lost to decay. Walk around the tomb to see how weather has aged its southern and western sides while leaving the rest nearly intact. Matthews earned his title by pioneering a process that mixed marble chips with sulphuric acid to make carbonic acid gas, which, combined with water, carbonated a beverage — essentially what we now call seltzer. By 1870 he was supplying more than five hundred soda fountains. His slogan: "Youth as it sips its first glass, experiences sensations which, like the first sensations of love, cannot be forgotten but are cherished to the last."

beats.script_body: Green-Wood had no chapel until the early twentieth century. When it solicited bids, Carrère & Hastings submitted a plan; rejected here, the firm modified it into what became the main branch of the New York Public Library at Forty-second Street and Fifth Avenue. The firm of Warren & Wetmore — best known for Grand Central Terminal, completed in 1913 — was chosen instead and built the chapel in 1912, a scaled-down version of Christopher Wren's Tom Tower at Christ Church, Oxford. After decades closed, the chapel reopened in April 2000; it is meant for individual contemplation but can be reserved for services. Alongside it stands the very large receiving tomb, its elaborate entrance echoing the cemetery's main gate. Capable of holding fifteen hundred bodies, it dates to the cemetery's earliest days: before modern digging equipment, those who died in winter, when the ground was frozen, were held here until the spring thaw. Its vast size is evident from the series of black metal vents along the hillside.

beats.script_body: Perhaps the New York Times said it best in 1866: "It is the ambition of the New Yorker to live on Fifth Avenue, to take his airings in the Park, and to sleep with his fathers in Green-Wood." Returning to where we began, we can ponder the lives of those buried here and the shortness and unpredictability of life. Fugit hora — the hours are fleeting.
